extracted.intended_audience: students, critics, and practitioners of aesthetics, literature, and the fine arts (writers, painters, poets, art critics)
extracted.subtask_description: Guiding principles for judging or producing works of imagination (poetry, painting, prose, etc.) based on the faculties of sense, imagination, and judgment; emphasizes universal principles of taste, the role of resemblance and sympathy, and the influence of knowledge and habit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Existence of Common Principles of Taste
rubrics_metrics.description: There are some principles of taste common to all mankind; without such principles no satisfactory reasoning about taste is possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay argues that a shared foundation for taste is necessary to discuss and teach taste reliably; if taste were mere caprice, laying down rules would be futile. Use these common principles as the basis for critique or instruction rather than treating taste as wholly subjective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Taste as Composite: Senses, Imagination, and Judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: Taste is 'partly made up of a perception of the primary pleasures of sense, of the secondary pleasures of the imagination, and of the conclusions of the reasoning faculty concerning the various relations of these, and concerning the human passions, manners, and actions.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating a work, attend to (1) sensory impact (colour, sound, tactile imagery), (2) imaginative pleasure (novel combinations, resemblance), and (3) rational/ethical judgment (probability, manners, decency). A full judgement of taste must integrate all three.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniformity of Natural Sensory Pleasures
rubrics_metrics.description: The pleasures and pains which every object excites in one man, it must raise in all mankind while it operates naturally; e.g., 'vinegar sour, honey sweet, and aloes bitter' are agreed upon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rely on natural, commonly shared sensory responses as baseline criteria (light more pleasing than darkness, summer preferable to winter visually). Anti-pattern: treating idiosyncratic, physiologically atypical responses as general standards (someone who cannot distinguish sweet from bitter indicates a vitiated sense, not a counterexample to common taste).

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish Natural from Acquired Tastes
rubrics_metrics.description: Custom and habit can alter relish, but we should 'distinguish to the last the acquired from the natural relish.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In criticism, separate pleasures due to learned association or habit (e.g., drug-induced tastes like opium or tobacco) from those arising from natural sensory qualities. Do not conflate culturally or habitually acquired preferences with universal standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imitation valued for Resemblance to the Original
rubrics_metrics.description: In the imagination 'a pleasure is perceived from the resemblance which the imitation has to the original.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For imitative arts (painting, realistic poetry, etc.), judge how well the work reproduces or resembles its object; pleasure derives both from the object's intrinsic properties and from the quality of likeness. Example: a novice admires a crude statue for general resemblance; the connoisseur values fidelity of detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pleasure in Tracing Resemblances (Wit) vs. Pleasure in Distinguishing (Judgment)
rubrics_metrics.description: The mind 'has naturally a far greater alacrity and satisfaction in tracing resemblances than in searching for differences'; wit excels at similitude, judgment at distinctions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Figures of speech, similes, and striking resemblances are intrinsically pleasing and more immediately effective on the imagination; however, sound critical judgment requires attending to differences, exactness, and probability. Use resemblance to engage the reader, but rely on critical distinctions for rigor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality as Recombination not Absolute Novelty
rubrics_metrics.description: The imagination 'is incapable of producing anything absolutely new; it can only vary the disposition of those ideas which it has received from the senses.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess originality by the novelty and force of recombination of sensory ideas rather than expecting metaphysical or absolute novelty. Innovation in imaginative work is judged by inventive arrangements of familiar elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Knowledge, Practice, and Attention Improve Critical Taste
rubrics_metrics.description: Critical taste 'does not depend upon a superior principle in men, but upon superior knowledge'; differences in taste often arise from differences in knowledge and attentive practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating fine distinctions (e.g., anatomical accuracy, proportion, or specialized craft), privileged deference should be given to experts (e.g., anatomist vs. painter vs. shoemaker). Training and close attention refine taste — foster domain knowledge to make finer judgments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish Lack of Sensibility from Faulty Judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: A defect in sensibility produces a want of taste; a weakness in judgment constitutes a wrong or bad taste.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Diagnose failures in aesthetic response: are they due to blunt sensibility (insensitivity to subtle pleasures) or to defective judgment (ignorance, prejudice, rashness)? Remedies differ: cultivate sensibility vs. educate the faculty of judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Propriety, Probability, and Manners as Elements of Taste
rubrics_metrics.description: What is called taste, by way of distinction, 'consists' in skill in manners, observances of time and place, and of decency in general — a refined judgment informed by philosophy and the world.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate imaginative works for observance of decorum, plausibility (probability), and appropriateness to context (time/place). Moral and social knowledge (manners, ethics) are part of the standard of taste.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of Sympathy and Representation of Passions
rubrics_metrics.description: Many passions 'are represented, because by the force of natural sympathy they are felt in all men without any recourse to reasoning, and their justness recognized in every breast.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Works that authentically represent common passions (love, grief, fear, joy, anger) will commonly elicit universal sympathy; use genuine representation of feeling to achieve broad impact rather than relying on obscure or eccentric states.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits of Comparative Judgement in Degrees
rubrics_metrics.description: Judgements about degrees of qualities (smoothness, polish, shades of color) lack a common measure and therefore are harder to settle except by obvious differences or by relying on specialists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be cautious about fine-grained comparative claims; employ measurable standards where possible, or defer to practitioners with refined habitual experience for subtle gradations. Avoid treating marginal differences as decisive without clear standardization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer Teaching that Reveals Method of Discovery
rubrics_metrics.description: The method of teaching 'which approaches most nearly to the method of investigation is incomparably the best; ... it tends to set the reader himself in the track of invention.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When instructing writers or artists, show processes, demonstrate how conclusions were reached, and guide learners toward independent invention rather than merely presenting barren maxims. Practical, discovery-oriented instruction improves taste and creativity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate Works by Both Common Response and Educated Appraisal
rubrics_metrics.description: While certain pleasures are common to all, differences in degree arise from natural sensibility or improved attention/knowledge; thus both popular response and critical (learned) appraisal matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In assessment, weigh universal, immediate responses (natural sympathy, sensory pleasure) alongside informed, critical judgments that draw on knowledge and trained perception. A comprehensive evaluation balances both perspectives.
